text.p: The following are the main stories from Monday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Members of opposition Social Democrats (SPD) call for vote to decide who will be their candidate for chancellor in 1998.
- Mystery surrounds whereabouts of kidnapped Frankfurt businessman after ransom paid for his freedom.
- Opposition Greens party holds strategy conference in Hanover.
- Former Stern publisher Henri Nannen dies aged 82.
- Social security contributions incur less tax than previously thought, a finance ministry report shows.
HANDELSBLATT
- Government plans cuts in some pensions, according to a Sunday newspaper report.
- No agreement in sight among governing coalition over proposals to tax life insurance.
- Gehe AG looking to sell off its generic drugs unit Azupharma, buyer likely to be Switzerland's Sandoz AG .
- Ifo institute predicts situation in jobs market will not get worse in 1997.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Interior Minister Manfred Kanther ready to compromise on his plans to change working conditions for civil servants.
- Greens' parliamentary leader Joschka Fischer urges party to concentrate on getting into power in 1998.
- Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) will get rid of 1,000 jobs fewer than originally planned, company chairman says.
DIE WELT
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem rejects suggestions of giving the jobless no benefit payments for the first week of their unemployment.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel plans final attempt to get agreement with opposition on next year's tax plans.
- Plans to increase postage prices remain controversial.
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl says he will not call together employers and union leaders to sort out row over sick pay.
